title: Module 1 · Managing in the Digital World
description: Interactive introduction to management information systems: the digital world and digital density, what an information system is, the dual nature of IS in organizational success and failure, computer ethics and information privacy, plus a clearly labeled strategy application supplement, and deciding where AI belongs in a business workflow.
hero:
Module 1

Managing in the Digital World

An information system is the combination of people and information technology that creates, collects, processes, stores, and distributes useful data. That one sentence is doing a lot of work, and this module unpacks all of it: the world these systems now run, what the parts actually are, why the same technology can make one company and break another, what responsible use of it looks like, and how a manager turns any of that into a decision worth defending.

How to use this page

  1. Read the short setup first. Every term is explained in ordinary language before any activity uses it, so nothing here assumes a background you have not been given yet.
  2. Answer as you go. The activities sit inside the reading, not at the end. When you answer a question, every option explains itself — including the three you did not pick, because knowing why a wrong answer is wrong is the part that transfers.
  3. Use the diagrams. The tabs redraw one idea from several angles. On a phone, a wide diagram scrolls sideways rather than shrinking to nothing.
  4. Retry anything. Restart one activity, one section, or the whole page. Your completion record stays in this browser until you clear it; the answers themselves reset on reload so you always get a fresh attempt.
  5. Finish with the final challenge. It unlocks once you have answered all thirty situations, then reports the four chapter objectives and the two application supplements separately so a weak area shows up instead of being averaged away.

Where this module sits in the course objectives

The three modules are organized around the textbook’s own learning objectives, but the course is graded against a different list. This table says plainly which of the eleven course objectives this module serves, and which ones it does not, so you always know why you are reading something.

Course objectiveWhat this module does with it
2. Discuss how companies use information systems to manage internal operations and to make decisions This module’s main job. Systems inside an organization works through the whole catalogue, from transaction processing up to decision support and enterprise-wide systems, and says which level of the business each one serves. What an information system is supplies the data, information and knowledge foundation underneath it, and the artificial-intelligence supplement adds the newest tool in that catalogue.
1. Describe what a company’s information systems department does Also central. The people in information systems covers the roles that group holds, the three competencies it hires for, and where an ordinary user fits. Systems inside an organization covers how the group is organized, who its staff report to, and why it now behaves more like an internal consultancy than a gatekeeper.
8. Describe the individual and organizational consequences of the use of information technology Also central. The digital world and digital density take the societal side; when systems succeed and fail takes the organizational one; ethics, privacy and property takes the personal duties of privacy, accuracy, property and access; and the artificial-intelligence supplement asks what the newest tools change about the work itself.
3. Discuss how companies use information technology for competitive advantage by changing their marketplace Substantial. When systems succeed and fail shows the same class of investment carrying one firm and sinking another, and the strategy supplement adds competitive forces, the value chain, and the four-part shape of a recommendation somebody can actually fund. Module 2 is where the same material becomes the whole subject.
7. Recognize a business problem which might be solved using information technology, then work with the information systems team on a solution The first half. Matching a complaint to the class of system that answers it, and carrying a finding through evidence to a named initiative and a measure, are both practiced here, and the working relationship with the information systems group is described. Developing and rolling out the system is not covered.
9. Recognize security breaches and computer crimes One kind of attack. Ransomware — what it does to data, why paying does not guarantee getting it back, and the backup, recovery and awareness practices that answer it — plus the duty to protect data against unauthorized access, disclosure or destruction. That is one attack and one duty, not a survey of computer crime.
4. Apply a working knowledge of computer hardware, software, database technology and computer networks Introduced only. What an information system is defines the technology half — hardware, software and telecommunications networks — and separates it from the people and organizational halves. The working knowledge itself is built in Module 3.
5. Delineate how businesses use internet technology for electronic commerce, communicating with employees and working with business partners Named, not developed. The catalogue defines the electronic-commerce, collaboration, customer-relationship and supply-chain systems that carry that work, one entry at a time. How the technology underneath them actually works is Module 3’s job.
6. Outline the life cycle of an information system Not taught here. The phrase appears once, in the list of what a systems competency covers, and nothing in this module explains or assesses it.
10. Solve a business problem by creating a database application using SQLite · 11. Use advanced spreadsheet functions to create a decision support system Served by the course’s separate database and spreadsheet work rather than by any reading module. This module defines what a decision support system is; building one is that separate work.
World

The setting

Ubiquitous computing, knowledge work, globalization, and the widening reach of connected devices.

System

The parts

Data becomes information becomes knowledge — carried by hardware, software, networks, and people.

Stakes

The double edge

The same investment that carries one company past its rivals can sink another. Both happen for reasons.

Judgment

The responsibility

Privacy, accuracy, property, access — and a method for recommending technology you can defend.

One idea connects the whole module Technology by itself is not the story. An information system is technology plus the people who use it and the organization it sits inside, and it is those last two parts that decide whether the first one is worth anything. That is why a company can buy exactly what its competitor bought and get a completely different result.

finalIntro:
Put it together

Final challenge

Thirty situations rather than thirty definitions. Each one presents a documented chapter case or a clearly hypothetical organizational situation and asks what is actually going on, which is the form the material takes once you are the person being asked. Answer all of them, then score: the result breaks out by chapter objective and supplement, so if one area is weak you will see exactly which section to reread instead of a single number that hides it.
foot: What to do next. Two things make this material stick. First, take one organization you already deal with — an employer, a store you shop at, a service you pay for — and name its information systems out loud: what data goes in, what information comes out, who acts on it. Second, practise the strategy method on that same organization until naming a force and an initiative feels routine. Everything after this chapter assumes both habits.
